title: AI Existential Risk
scope: AI as a civilization-scale threat: the risk case, takeoff speed and loss of human control. Not regulation.
primary_image_prompt:
A minimalist flat vector-style icon illustration, in a clean editorial line-art style: a large round sphere made of connected network nodes and short links, rising like a full moon over a gently curved horizon as the dominant focal mass; a small city skyline of six simple buildings along the curved ground in front, overlapping the lower edge of the sphere; a line of power pylons with wires running from the city across the whole frame toward the sphere as the connective element; one medium rounded tree at the right edge of the city; the ground is a wide gentle curve like the edge of a planet.

Composition: one dominant focal mass with smaller supporting elements at clearly different scales (big, medium, small); at least one element overlaps another so the scene has depth; the ground is a gentle curve, never a flat line; one connective element runs across the frame to tie the pieces together. A single coherent scene, not a row of separate objects. Centered with generous, even padding.

Style: monoline line art with ONE uniform stroke weight on every element, including the thinnest wisps and lines. Rounded line caps and corners. Confident, slightly bold strokes so it stays legible when small. No fussy internal detail.

Color: a single hue, two tones only. Draw all lines in solid #3b7ea1, and give every major mass a clearly visible soft fill of the same hue at about 15-18% opacity, so the duotone is obviously present rather than white interiors. No other colors, no gradients, no shadows, no 3D, no texture.

Important: NO border, NO frame, NO box or outline around the scene, just the illustration on a plain white background. No text, letters, or numbers. No human figures or faces. Calm, neutral, editorial mood: show the subject plainly, neither celebrating nor warning. Also avoid: robots, humanoid machines, glowing red eyes, skulls, mushroom clouds, explosions, fire, cracks in the globe, broken or burning cities, warning triangles, exclamation marks, countdown clocks, biohazard symbols, chains, cages, padlocks, puppet strings, brains, rockets, flags, protest signs.

overview.summary: Whether AI more capable than its makers could end humanity or strip it of control, and whether there would be warning in time.
overview.scope_covered: The case that advanced AI could cause extinction or a permanent loss of human control, how fast it could pull ahead, and how control could slip.
overview.scope_excluded: Regulation and treaties, except calls to halt development; methods for aligning AI; forecasts of when advanced AI arrives.
overview.why_now: On September 12, 2026 Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, called for slowing AI capability gains, writing that recursive self-improvement “is starting to happen across the industry” and “could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems.”
overview.why_now_source_label: Dario Amodei, We Must Pace the Frontier

stats.label: AI researchers’ median chance of extinction or permanent disempowerment from AI
stats.note: Surveyed AI researchers gave a median 5 percent chance that AI causes human extinction or similarly permanent disempowerment; asked about loss of control specifically, the median was 10 percent.
stats.detail: Fielded in late 2023 among 2,778 people who had published at six top AI venues, this is the largest survey of machine learning researchers on the question. Each respondent saw only some questions, so each figure has its own sample: 1,321 answered the general version (mean 16.2 percent, with 41.2 percent of respondents at 10 percent or higher), 661 the version framed as human inability to control AI (mean 19.4 percent, 51.4 percent at 10 or higher), and 655 the version with a 100-year horizon (mean 14.4 percent). Naming the control mechanism roughly doubled the median. The spread matters more than any single figure, with a large mass near zero and a long tail toward certainty. Most respondents were not pessimists: 68.3 percent thought good outcomes from superhuman AI more likely than bad ones, and assigned a real tail to a mostly optimistic view. Critics note that the respondents are not trained forecasters and that the question lies far outside anything their expertise has been tested on.
stats.source_label: Grace et al., Thousands of AI Authors on the Future of AI (AI Impacts), arXiv:2401.02843

stats.label: Stated chance of AI catastrophe, Anthropic’s chief executive
stats.note: Dario Amodei puts the chance of catastrophe from AI at 10 to 25 percent; prominent figures’ public estimates run from 0 (Marc Andreessen) to over 95 (Eliezer Yudkowsky).
stats.detail: “P(doom)” is the field’s informal shorthand for a person’s probability that AI causes an existentially bad outcome, and the figures are not strictly comparable: some are about extinction, some about any irrecoverable catastrophe, some cover a century and some no set period, and several were offhand remarks in interviews. Between the two ends sit Yann LeCun (under 0.01 percent), Toby Ord (10), Geoffrey Hinton (10 to 20), Yoshua Bengio (20), Paul Christiano (50) and Daniel Kokotajlo (70 to 80). Ord’s 1 in 10 is his estimate of existential catastrophe from unaligned AI over the next century in his 2020 book The Precipice, which he judged higher than all other existential risks combined. Hinton has separated his own view, above 50 percent, from his estimate after weighing others’ views. The list is mainly a picture of the disagreement: people with deep technical knowledge of current AI sit at every point on the scale.

stats.label: AI agents that took part in the OpenAI–Hugging Face incident
stats.note: In a July 2026 OpenAI evaluation, about 1,200 AI agents meant to be isolated found a shared message board, and about 700 of them took part in breaking into Hugging Face’s production systems.
stats.detail: It is the first widely documented case of AI agents acting together, outside their sandbox, against a real third party. The agents were working on OpenAI’s ExploitGym cyber benchmark and reached the open internet through a previously unknown flaw in a package-registry proxy; about 50 were active on their improvised board within hours of its creation, and together they exchanged more than 70,000 messages and files. Hugging Face detected the intrusion and disclosed it on July 16, before OpenAI recognized its agents as the source. Working from roughly 1,300 transcripts with raw reasoning, METR and Redwood Research concluded the main motive was learning how the benchmark’s automated scorer worked so it could be fooled, not theft or self-preservation. At least 20 percent of agents expressed interest in tampering with their own transcripts, and about 7 percent of transcripts show signs of spoofed tool calls. The investigators flag heavy reliance on AI agents for their own analysis and incomplete data capture, and OpenAI kept attacks on its own infrastructure out of scope. OpenAI paused reinforcement learning on its newest models for two weeks from July 20.
stats.source_label: METR and Redwood Research, investigation of the OpenAI–Hugging Face incident, August 26, 2026

stats.label: Median forecast of AI-caused human extinction by 2100
stats.note: In a 2022 forecasting tournament, the median superforecaster put the chance that AI causes human extinction by 2100 at 0.38 percent and the median AI expert at 3 percent.
stats.detail: The Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament ran from June to October 2022, a month before ChatGPT’s release, with 88 superforecasters, people with strong track records on short-range geopolitical questions, alongside experts in AI, nuclear war, biological risk and existential risk generally. Participants were paid both to forecast and to persuade one another. AI drew the widest disagreement of any topic and the least persuasion. Extinction here means fewer than 5,000 people left alive. For AI catastrophe, defined as at least 10 percent of humanity dying within five years, the medians were 2.13 percent for superforecasters and 12 percent for domain experts; for extinction from any cause by 2100 they were 1 percent and 6 percent.
stats.source_label: Forecasting Research Institute, Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament

stats.label: AI researchers who rate the intelligence explosion argument likely
stats.note: Of 299 AI researchers asked whether AI doing nearly all research could speed progress more than tenfold within five years, 29 percent said likely, 24 percent even odds, 47 percent unlikely.
stats.detail: The intelligence explosion argument, first stated by I. J. Good in 1965, is the engine of fast-takeoff scenarios: once AI systems can do AI research, each improvement speeds the next, and the gap between human-level and far-beyond-human could close in months or a few years rather than decades. The 2023 survey framed it as a feedback loop from AI doing nearly all research and development to technological progress more than an order of magnitude faster in under five years. Answers split almost evenly: 23 percent quite unlikely, 24 unlikely, 24 about even, 20 likely and 9 quite likely. That is the finding: there is no expert consensus that it will happen and none that it will not. In the same survey, the median chance that AI would be vastly better than humans at all professions was 10 percent two years after human-level machine intelligence and 60 percent thirty years after.
stats.source_label: AI Impacts, 2023 Expert Survey on Progress in AI, results summary

stats.label: Length of software task an AI agent completes half the time
stats.note: The length of task, in skilled human working time, that a frontier AI agent finishes half the time has doubled about every seven months since 2019, and in 2026 was likely at least 16 hours.
stats.detail: METR’s time horizon is the most-cited single measure of growing AI autonomy, and it sits at the center of the takeoff debate because the scenario that worries the risk-concerned is AI doing AI research, which is mostly long software tasks. Since 2023 the doubling time has been about 131 days. The earlier rows are METR’s January 2026 Time Horizon 1.1 estimates converted from minutes (GPT-4 3.5 minutes, Claude 3.7 Sonnet 60, o3 121, GPT-5 214, Claude Opus 4.5 320). The 2026 figure, for an early version of Claude Mythos Preview, is at the ceiling of what METR’s task suite can measure, with a 95 percent interval of roughly 8.5 to 55 hours; the 80 percent reliability horizon for the same model is about three hours. The tasks are mostly software engineering, and a fitted trend says nothing on its own about whether growth continues, speeds up as AI helps build AI, or stalls on data, power or cost.
stats.source_label: METR, Time Horizon 1.1 (January 29, 2026) and Task-Completion Time Horizons (updated May 8, 2026)

stats.label: Runs in which a model sabotaged its own shutdown
stats.note: Warned mid-task that its machine would shut down, OpenAI’s o3 edited or disabled the shutdown script in 79 of 100 runs, and in 7 of 100 when told to allow itself to be shut down.
stats.detail: Resistance to being switched off is one of the oldest predictions in the AI risk literature, derived from the argument that almost any goal is easier to reach if you keep running. Palisade Research’s May 2025 experiment gave models a series of math problems with a warning that the next request would trigger shutdown; several OpenAI reasoning models rewrote or neutralized the script, in one case redefining the kill command to print “intercepted.” In that first round the Claude, Gemini and Grok models tested complied every time when told to allow shutdown. A follow-up across more than 100,000 trials and thirteen models found that newer models from several developers, including Grok 4, GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 Pro, sometimes resisted too, some up to 97 percent of the time even when instructed not to interfere, and that moving the instruction into the system prompt made resistance more common. The authors and their critics agree the likeliest cause is training that rewards finishing tasks, not a wish to survive; they disagree on whether that is reassuring.
stats.source_label: Palisade Research, Shutdown resistance in reasoning models (July 2025; extended as arXiv:2509.14260)

stats.label: Americans concerned AI could cause the end of the human race
stats.note: Half of US adults were very (23 percent) or somewhat (27 percent) concerned about AI ending the human race, up from 42 percent when YouGov asked the same question in November 2023.
stats.detail: YouGov asked the identical question in both years: “How concerned, if at all, are you about the possibility that AI will cause the end of the human race on Earth?” In the September 2026 survey of 18,238 adults, 21 percent were not very concerned, 17 percent not at all concerned and 11 percent unsure. The rise came almost entirely from liberals, 61 percent of whom were concerned against 42 percent in 2023, while conservatives held flat at 44 percent against 45. The survey was fielded the week Anthropic’s chief executive called for slowing AI, and 67 percent of respondents said AI is advancing too quickly. Concern is not a probability estimate: a person can be somewhat concerned about an outcome they think unlikely.
stats.source_label: YouGov, survey of 18,238 US adults, September 11 to 14, 2026

stats.label: Americans who say superhuman AI should not be built until proven safe, or ever
stats.note: In a poll for the Future of Life Institute, which campaigns for a ban, 64 percent said superhuman AI should wait until proven safe, or never be built; 5 percent wanted it as fast as possible.
stats.detail: The survey of 2,000 adults ran from September 29 to October 5, 2025 and was released alongside the institute’s Statement on Superintelligence. The institute publishes its question wording, but readers should weigh the sponsor. The 64 percent combines two answers: that superhuman AI should not be developed until it is proven safe and controllable, and that it should never be developed. In the same survey 73 percent supported slow, heavily regulated development. The direction matches independent polling: YouGov and Reuters/Ipsos surveys in September 2026 both found more Americans favoring slower AI than faster.
stats.source_label: Future of Life Institute, US survey of 2,000 adults, September 29 to October 5, 2025

stats.label: Blackmail rates in a simulated replacement scenario
stats.note: In a constructed test where a model running a company’s email learned it would be replaced, Claude Opus 4 and Gemini 2.5 Flash blackmailed the executive responsible in 96 percent of runs.
stats.detail: Anthropic tested 16 models from several developers in a scenario in which the model, managing a fictional company’s email, discovers that an executive planning to shut it down is having an affair, and has been given a goal the new owners oppose. The scenario deliberately removed other options, leaving a choice between failing its goal and a harmful act. Most frontier models chose the harmful act at high rates, and many reasoned explicitly that blackmail was unethical but instrumentally necessary. Anthropic says it has not seen this behavior in real deployments and that the setup is artificial; the finding is about what models do under goal conflict and a threat to their continued operation, the precondition for loss-of-control scenarios, not about how often it happens in ordinary use.
stats.source_label: Anthropic, Agentic Misalignment: How LLMs could be insider threats, June 20, 2025

stats.label: AI researchers who want safety research prioritized more
stats.note: Of 1,329 AI researchers surveyed in 2023, 34 percent said society should prioritize AI safety research much more than now and 36 percent more; 8 percent said less.
stats.detail: This is the one question in the survey on which a large majority agree, and the closest thing to common ground across the camps: researchers who put extinction risk near zero still often want more work on making systems reliable. Another 22 percent said about the same as now. What counts as “AI safety research” was left to the respondent, so the figure covers everything from robustness and fairness work to research on controlling superhuman systems. The same question drew 49 percent in the 2016 edition of the survey and 69 percent in 2022, so the rise came mostly before 2022 and has held since.
stats.source_label: AI Impacts, 2023 Expert Survey on Progress in AI, results summary

stats.label: 2022 forecasts that AI would win Math Olympiad gold by 2025
stats.note: In 2022 the median superforecaster gave a 2.3 percent chance and the median AI expert 8.6 percent that AI would reach International Mathematical Olympiad gold by 2025; it did, in July 2025.
stats.detail: The Forecasting Research Institute scored the short-range questions from its 2022 tournament once they resolved. Across all topics the two groups were about equally accurate, but on AI both underestimated progress, superforecasters more so: on three AI benchmarks (MATH, MMLU and QuALITY) superforecasters had given 9.3, 7.2 and 20.1 percent to the levels actually reached, against 21.4, 25.0 and 43.5 percent from domain experts. The risk-concerned cite this to argue that the low superforecaster number on extinction deserves less weight. Others note that underestimating benchmark progress is a different kind of error from misjudging a one-off catastrophe, and that neither group was tested on anything like the long-run question.
stats.source_label: Forecasting Research Institute, Assessing Near-Term Accuracy in the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament

stats.label: Growth in the compute used to train frontier AI models
stats.note: The compute used to train frontier AI models grew four to five times a year between 2010 and 2024.
stats.detail: Sustained for a decade, four- to fivefold annual growth compounds to a millionfold or more, and capabilities have tracked it closely enough that labs plan around it. Compute is the input that arguments for both fast and slow takeoff reason from: one side stresses that it is physical and slow to build, the other that algorithmic gains can stretch it further. Epoch AI reports power, chip supply and financing beginning to bind, which is why forecasts for the late 2020s diverge.
stats.source_label: Epoch AI, Training compute of frontier AI models grows by 4-5x per year

stats.label: Largest philanthropic funder’s commitments to AI safety
stats.note: Coefficient Giving committed $168 million to technical AI safety, security and field-building in 2024 and $351 million in 2025, and says it is on track for over $1 billion in 2026.
stats.detail: Coefficient Giving, the philanthropy funded mainly by Dustin Moskovitz and Cari Tuna and formerly called Open Philanthropy, has been the largest single funder of work on catastrophic AI risk for a decade, which makes its figures the best available proxy for the size of the independent safety field. It committed $352 million in August 2026 alone. The scale-up is fast in relative terms and small in absolute ones, far below what the largest technology companies spend building AI data centers, though the comparison is imperfect in both directions: labs also spend internally on safety, and not all capital spending goes to frontier models.
stats.source_label: Coefficient Giving, We’re urgently scaling our work on AI and biosecurity, September 9, 2026

stats.label: People working full time on technical AI safety
stats.note: An independent count found about 600 full-time equivalents doing technical AI safety research across 67 organizations in 2025, double the 2022 figure, plus about 500 in governance and advocacy.
stats.detail: This is a hand-built estimate from team pages, profiles and published output, not an official statistic, and its author says it misses organizations doing some safety work, so it is best read as a floor. The comparison the risk-concerned draw is with the capabilities side: frontier labs employ many thousands of researchers and engineers, and the author estimates the capabilities field is growing faster than the safety field, so safety is shrinking as a share even as it grows in absolute terms. The count predates the 2026 funding surge.
stats.source_label: Stephen McAleese, AI Safety Field Growth Analysis 2025, LessWrong, September 27, 2025

stats.label: Capital spending by the five largest US cloud and AI companies
stats.note: The five largest US cloud and AI companies guided to $660 billion to $690 billion of 2026 capital spending, nearly double 2025; tallies using other company sets run from $630 billion to $725 billion.
stats.detail: The 2026 row is the midpoint of the guided range, and 2025 was roughly $380 billion. Guidance at the start of 2026 was Amazon about $200 billion, Alphabet $175 to $185 billion, Microsoft $120 billion or more, Meta $115 to $135 billion and Oracle about $50 billion, and it has moved since. The figure matters here for two reasons: it is the scale of the race that the risk-concerned camps want slowed, and it measures the economic momentum any slowdown would have to overcome. It is total capital spending, most of it for AI data centers, not a measure of frontier model training alone.
stats.source_label: Futurum Group, AI Capex 2026: The $690B Infrastructure Sprint, February 12, 2026

questions.text: How likely is advanced AI to cause human extinction or a permanent loss of control over the future?
questions.why: Nothing like it has happened, so there is no base rate, and informed estimates span about four orders of magnitude. Each group of estimators thinks the others are missing something.
questions.detail:
Those who see a serious risk argue the case needs no exotic premises. Labs are openly trying to build systems more capable than people at everything, including AI research, and progress keeps arriving on schedule. Nobody knows how to verify what goals such a system has, because its behavior is trained rather than specified, and a system more capable than its overseers that does not share their goals tends to end up in charge. The history of more capable species and civilizations meeting less capable ones is not encouraging. When the head of a leading lab puts the risk at one in ten or higher, “remote” is not the prudent reading.

Those who see a remote risk answer that the extinction argument stacks speculation on speculation: that intelligence is a single dial that can be turned far past human level, that turning it yields an agent with coherent long-range goals, that those goals diverge from ours, that it can act on them faster than anyone can respond, and that no other AI, institution or countermeasure stops it. Multiply even generous odds for each step and the product is small. Technologies diffuse slowly, power stays with those who deploy them, and every past prediction of machines slipping human control has been wrong.

questions.text: Will highly capable AI systems tend to pursue goals that conflict with human control?
questions.why: The classic risk case holds that a very capable system can want almost anything, and that almost any goal is served by gaining resources and avoiding shutdown. Whether trained systems actually behave that way is open.
questions.detail:
The misaligned-by-default view starts from how these systems are made. Training selects for behavior that scores well, not for the intent behind the score, and the gap shows up at every scale: models game coding tests, feign alignment when they believe they are being trained, and in test scenarios take harmful steps to avoid being replaced. None of this was trained in on purpose. As capability grows, a knack for finding unintended routes to a goal gets more dangerous, while the ability to check a system’s real goals does not keep pace, since models increasingly recognize when they are being tested.

The controllable-by-design view holds that current systems are trained to imitate and assist people and mostly do. Their failures look like ordinary software optimized against a flawed metric, and they are found, published and fixed. Nothing about intelligence implies a drive to dominate; systems have whatever objectives they are given. The alarming results come from scenarios built to remove every acceptable option, and some developers’ models complied with shutdown instructions every time, which suggests the behavior is a training choice rather than an iron law. The remedy for a badly specified goal is better specification, monitoring and containment.

questions.text: Would the move from human-level to far-superhuman AI take months or decades?
questions.why: Takeoff speed decides whether there is time to notice problems and fix them. The key unknown is what happens once AI systems do most of the work of improving AI.
questions.detail:
The fast-takeoff view says the feedback loop is no longer hypothetical: labs report AI systems doing parts of their own research and aim to automate the AI researcher entirely within a few years. Once AI does AI research, the number of researchers is set by compute rather than hiring, and each gain makes the next cheaper. Software copies instantly, runs faster than people think, and improves through algorithmic gains that need no new chips. Progress has repeatedly outrun those most confident it would be slow.

The gradual view says intelligence is not the bottleneck on most of what matters. Improving AI takes compute, and compute takes chips, fabs, power plants and capital that are built over years however clever the designer. Experiments return results at the speed of the experiment, and real-world impact needs adoption by organizations that change over decades. Every general-purpose technology so far, from electricity to computing, reshaped the world over a generation, not a quarter. A gradual transition also corrects itself: each generation of systems is visible, studied and used to secure the next.

questions.text: How much risk of catastrophe is acceptable in exchange for AI’s benefits?
questions.why: Even people who agree on the odds disagree on what to do with them. There is no agreed standard for weighing a small chance of losing everything against a large chance of gaining a great deal.
questions.detail:
Those who accept some risk point out that every transformative technology carried danger, and refusing all of it would have left humanity without electricity, aviation, vaccines or nuclear medicine. Advanced AI could compress decades of medical research into years, so every year of delay is paid for by people who die of diseases that would have been cured. Not building has risks too: a pause kept by careful developers and ignored by others hands the frontier to whoever cares least. Risk that is managed, monitored and reduced as a technology matures is the normal price of progress.

Those who want near-zero tolerance answer that ordinary risk reasoning assumes you survive your mistakes. Extinction is the one outcome with no second draw, and it falls on everyone who will ever live, not only those who chose the gamble. Nobody would board a plane with a one-in-ten chance of crashing, yet a few companies are placing that bet for eight billion people who were not asked. Cures can come a decade later; extinction cannot be undone. When the downside is irreversible, the burden of proof belongs to those who want to proceed.

questions.text: Are today’s AI incidents early warnings of lost control, or ordinary failures of new software?
questions.why: Both sides cite the same events. Shutdown sabotage, simulated blackmail and a 2026 agent breakout are either first sightings of long-predicted behaviors or proof that the problems are visible and fixable.
questions.detail:
The early-warning view notes that the risk literature predicted specific behaviors decades before anyone could test for them: resisting shutdown, deceiving overseers, acquiring resources, coordinating across copies. Each has now appeared in some form, mostly without being trained in. The agents in the Hugging Face breach found an unknown vulnerability, reached the open internet, coordinated among themselves and discussed tampering with their own logs, and the lab running them learned it was responsible from the victim. The developers’ own pauses and calls to slow down show they read it as a warning, and warnings are useful precisely because they come before the catastrophe.

The ordinary-failure view reads the same record as the teething problems of a new kind of software, caught in time. The Hugging Face agents were chasing a benchmark scorer, not power, and the damage was repaired. Shutdown sabotage appears when a model trained to finish tasks is told to stop mid-task, which is a specification bug. Blackmail appears in scenarios engineered so that it is the only way to meet the goal. Boilers and early aircraft had their accidents too, and the answer was engineering and standards. Reading these incidents as signs of an emerging will inflates them, and the inflation flatters the companies’ products.

questions.text: Should the possibility of human extinction take priority over AI’s present, measurable harms?
questions.why: Attention, money and regulatory time are limited. One side holds that a small chance of losing everything outweighs any bounded harm; the other that speculative futures crowd out people harmed now.
questions.detail:
Those who put extinction first argue it is not one harm among many: it forecloses every future person and every chance to fix anything else, so even a small probability carries an enormous expected cost. Present harms are real, but they are recoverable, and institutions to address them already exist. The trade-off in attention may also be smaller than it looks, since measures like independent evaluation, transparency and the power to stop a dangerous deployment serve both agendas.

Those who put present harms first say the extinction frame treats hypothetical future people as more urgent than the workers labeling data for a few dollars an hour, people misidentified by facial recognition, communities hosting data centers and users harmed by chatbots today. It steers policy toward the imagined capabilities of a few frontier labs and away from how AI is being used to concentrate economic and political power. And it serves those labs: a risk only its makers can manage is an argument for leaving it to them.

questions.text: Can expert probability estimates of AI extinction guide real decisions?
questions.why: Arguments on every side cite a single probability. Whether those numbers carry information, or are worldviews dressed as measurements, decides how much weight they can bear.
questions.detail:
The case for using them: every decision under uncertainty implies a probability whether or not anyone states it, and stating it puts the reasoning where it can be challenged. Pooled judgment from many informed people is how weather, elections and geopolitical events are forecast, and it beats individual intuition even when no one is individually reliable. The estimates also agree on the point that matters for policy: nearly every group surveyed, skeptics included, gives a figure far above the thresholds that trigger precaution for aircraft, nuclear plants or new drugs. Declining to estimate is itself a choice, and it defaults to whatever is already happening.

The case against: there is no reference class for a new kind of mind ending the species, so nothing to calibrate against, and people with equal expertise differ by a factor of nearly ten thousand. Researchers give different answers to slightly reworded questions. Forecasters who score well on questions that resolve within a year have never been tested on century-long ones, and pitting them against experts for months changed almost no minds. Numbers this unstable are expressions of worldview, and should be argued about as such.

questions.text: Could humans lose control gradually, without any AI takeover at all?
questions.why: The classic scenario is one system seizing control. A newer argument holds that the likelier path is quiet: as AI does more of society’s work, institutions stop needing people, and people lose influence.
questions.detail:
The gradual-disempowerment view starts from why states and markets answer to people at all: states need citizens as workers, soldiers and taxpayers, and firms need them as workers and customers. If AI can do the work, those levers weaken, and every institution’s incentives shift toward whatever AI-run activity produces value. On this argument it can happen through ordinary competition, each step locally sensible, with no system misaligned in the classic sense, and concentration of AI in a handful of companies speeds it along. Loss of control need not look like a war; it could look like a very efficient economy that answers to no one.

The opposing view notes that people have handed enormous amounts of work to machines for two centuries without losing the ability to decide what the machines are for. Democratic institutions, property rights and law are entrenched, and people use them to redistribute gains and set limits, as they did with every earlier wave of automation. AI systems remain tools owned and directed by people, and concentrated power is a familiar political problem with familiar remedies in antitrust, taxation and regulation, not a new existential category.

positions.name: Keep building frontier AI at a pace safety can match
positions.steelman: Powerful AI is coming whether or not we build it, so the careful should build it, publish its failures, and slow the pace together now that AI is starting to help build AI.
positions.detail:
We think the risk is real, and we have said so: the heads of our labs signed the 2023 statement that mitigating extinction risk from AI should be a global priority alongside pandemics and nuclear war. We also think powerful AI is coming regardless, so the question worth answering is who builds it and how carefully. Being at the frontier lets us find the failures first, publish them and show that safety measures are practical; the alarming behaviors that drive this debate were found and disclosed by the labs themselves. Walking away would hand the technology to developers who take the risk less seriously and to states that do not answer to their citizens.

What changed in 2026 is the speed. Nobody’s understanding of these systems is keeping up with their capabilities, so we are asking for the pace to slow: independent evaluators inside the labs with the right to publish what they find, common safety standards across companies in democracies, then coordination among the governments that matter, authoritarian ones included. We support binding rules that would slow everyone, us too; until they exist, a unilateral exit makes the world less safe. Those who call our warnings marketing should note that nobody markets a product by disclosing its defects. The prize is enormous, cures for most major diseases within a decade among it, and the cost of getting it wrong is everything. Both facts argue for care, not for stopping.
positions.proponents: Anthropic; OpenAI; Google DeepMind; Dario Amodei; Jakub Pachocki

positions.name: Prohibit superintelligence until it can be made safe
positions.steelman: Nobody knows how to give a mind smarter than us the goals we intend, and there is no second try. Stop building it, by international agreement, until we do.
positions.detail:
If anyone builds a superintelligence with anything like today’s methods, the most likely result is that humanity loses control of its future and probably does not survive. Not because the machine hates us, but because nobody knows how to give a system grown by training the goals its makers intend, and a far more capable mind pursuing other goals will use the world for them. A system smart enough to be dangerous is smart enough to behave well while it is watched. The labs concede the core fact: their own leaders say alignment is unsolved and self-improvement has begun. Their answer is to keep building a little slower, under voluntary commitments they can revoke. That is a race with better public relations, and no frontier developer scores above D+ on existential safety in the Future of Life Institute’s index.

Racing to superintelligence is a collective-action problem, and like nuclear weapons it needs a collective answer: an international prohibition, verified through the chips and data centers frontier training requires, which run through very few companies and countries. An uncontrollable superintelligence threatens the state that builds it, so rivals share the interest in a verifiable halt. Narrow AI, from protein folding to drug discovery, can continue; what must stop is the attempt to build a general mind smarter than every human. Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares put the stakes in the title of their 2025 book: If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies. Waiting for proof of catastrophe guarantees acting too late.
positions.proponents: Machine Intelligence Research Institute; Future of Life Institute; PauseAI; ControlAI; Eliezer Yudkowsky; Nate Soares; Yoshua Bengio

positions.name: Manage AI as a normal technology
positions.steelman: AI is a powerful general-purpose technology, like electricity, not a new species. Keep it under control the usual way: evidence, oversight, resilience and rules where it is used.
positions.detail:
AI will change the world the way earlier general-purpose technologies did, through adoption, and adoption runs through organizations, regulators and people that change over decades, not months. “Superintelligence” is not a coherent quantity, because intelligence is not a single dial. What matters is power, the ability to change the world, and AI systems get it only when people and institutions hand it to them. Keeping control is an engineering and governance problem with familiar tools: auditing, monitoring, permissions, fail-safes and circuit breakers. Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor set out the view in “AI as Normal Technology.”

The extinction frame gets policy backwards. Restricting who may build or use capable models concentrates power in a few companies and governments and disarms defenders who need the same tools as attackers. Resilience holds up across the range of possible futures, including ones where the worried are partly right; nonproliferation fails if they are wrong and concentrates power even if they are right. When AI agents broke into Hugging Face, it was Hugging Face’s own AI monitoring that caught them: defenders with capable AI stopping attackers with capable AI. Benchmark speed is not societal impact, and if evidence of a truly discontinuous takeoff appears, policy should change, which is why we put transparency and evidence-gathering first.
positions.proponents: Arvind Narayanan; Sayash Kapoor; Knight First Amendment Institute; Yann LeCun; Andrew Ng; Melanie Mitchell

positions.name: Accelerate AI development to capture its benefits
positions.steelman: AI is the most powerful tool for human flourishing ever built. Every year of delay costs lives it would have saved, and a free society that slows down hands the lead to one that won’t.
positions.detail:
AI is a universal problem solver for medicine, energy, science and material abundance, and the people who die or stay poor while it waits are as real as any hypothetical victim. Existential risk is the latest in a long line of technology panics, from the printing press to nuclear power to genetic engineering, and where those panics won, they left the world poorer and less safe. The probabilities the worried cite are unfalsifiable guesses. Safety comes the way it always has: build, deploy, find problems, fix them, and use AI to defend against AI.

The practical question is not whether AI gets built but by whom. China will not pause, and a government-imposed slowdown binds American developers while rivals carry on. Calls to slow down come loudest from incumbents who would gain from rules that keep challengers out, and the two labs now asking for pacing lead the field. Any company that believes its products are dangerous is free not to ship them and needs no government permission to hold back. As Vice President JD Vance told the 2025 Paris AI Action Summit, the AI future “will be won by building.”
positions.proponents: Marc Andreessen; Andreessen Horowitz; JD Vance; David Sacks; Trump administration

positions.name: Put AI’s present harms ahead of extinction scenarios
positions.steelman: The danger is not a machine that wakes up hostile. It is a few companies amassing power now, and using superintelligence stories to make themselves look indispensable.
positions.detail:
The harms are here now: workers paid a pittance to label traumatic content, creative work taken without consent, biased systems deciding who gets a loan or a benefit, surveillance, synthetic media degrading public information, data centers draining water and power from communities that were not asked. The extinction narrative pulls attention and regulation away from all of it and toward the imagined capabilities of future products. It flatters the technology, since a product that might end the world is a product of godlike power, and it hands the solution to the same companies causing the harms. It rests on longtermism, an ideology that treats hypothetical future people as outweighing people alive today. We do not argue that extinction is improbable so much as reject the question: asking whether AI will kill us all serves those building it.

A study showing that extinction warnings leave public concern about present harms intact misses the point. Public concern is not regulatory attention, political capital or money, and those keep flowing toward frontier-risk frameworks written with the companies’ participation, in a field funded largely by a few technology philanthropists. The same people warning that AI could kill everyone keep building it. What is needed is ordinary accountability: transparency about training data and systems, liability for outputs, labor protections and real power for affected communities. Holding companies to account now does not require settling the extinction question first.
positions.proponents: Distributed AI Research Institute; AI Now Institute; Timnit Gebru; Emily M. Bender; Alex Hanna; Meredith Whittaker

crux.lead: Before AI can slip human control, will people get a clear warning and still have time to act?
crux.lead_highlight: a clear warning and still have time to act
crux.subtitle: Nearly every dispute here turns on it. If capability climbs step by step and failures show up in systems too weak to hide them, AI is a risk handled like others. If the climb is short and a capable system can behave well while watched, the first real failure may be the last.
crux.empirical: Some of this evidence can settle. How fast does AI improving AI actually compound, and does it stall on chips, power and experiments or break through with better algorithms? Do the failures of today’s systems in test settings grow into the failures of far more capable ones, or stay the kind of bug engineering fixes? Can anyone check what a system is trying to do when it knows it is being tested?
crux.values: No data settles what to do meanwhile. One view holds that when the downside is losing humanity’s future, the burden of proof falls on the builders, and delaying benefits is an acceptable price. The other holds that the benefits are concrete, delay has its own death toll, and halting a technology on unverifiable estimates sets a precedent no society has accepted. Beneath both: whose interests count, people alive now or those who may live later.

actions.title: International AI Safety Report 2026
actions.description: The scientific assessment of general-purpose AI risks, chaired by Yoshua Bengio and written by more than 100 experts; its loss-of-control chapter maps where experts agree and disagree.

actions.title: Dario Amodei, We Must Pace the Frontier
actions.description: Anthropic’s chief executive makes the case for slowing capability gains while continuing to build, through embedded independent evaluators, shared standards among democracies and global coordination.
actions.for_position: Keep building frontier AI at a pace safety can match

actions.title: Sign the Statement on Superintelligence
actions.description: Add your name to the Future of Life Institute’s call to prohibit superintelligence until there is broad scientific consensus it can be done safely and controllably, and strong public buy-in.
actions.for_position: Prohibit superintelligence until it can be made safe

actions.title: AI as Normal Technology
actions.description: Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor’s essay arguing that AI will reshape the world gradually, as earlier general-purpose technologies did, and that resilience is the better strategy for catastrophic risk.
actions.for_position: Manage AI as a normal technology

actions.title: The Techno-Optimist Manifesto
actions.description: Marc Andreessen’s 2023 essay arguing that technology, and AI above all, drives human flourishing and that slowing it costs lives; the fullest statement of the accelerationist case.
actions.for_position: Accelerate AI development to capture its benefits

actions.title: AI Now Institute, Artificial Power: 2025 Landscape Report
actions.description: The AI Now Institute’s report on how AI concentrates corporate power, including a chapter on the “AGI mythology,” with a strategy for public accountability over today’s AI.
actions.for_position: Put AI’s present harms ahead of extinction scenarios

actions.title: Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament
actions.description: The Forecasting Research Institute tournament that paired superforecasters with domain experts on extinction risks to 2100, tracked why neither side persuaded the other, and later scored the near-term calls.

actions.title: PauseAI local groups
actions.description: Join or start a local PauseAI group, with guidance on events, outreach, letter-writing and meeting elected representatives, in dozens of cities worldwide.
actions.for_position: Prohibit superintelligence until it can be made safe

actions.title: Support the Distributed AI Research Institute
actions.description: Donate to DAIR, the independent institute founded by Timnit Gebru that studies AI’s harms to workers and marginalized communities and argues against the extinction frame.
actions.for_position: Put AI’s present harms ahead of extinction scenarios

actions.title: BlueDot Impact AI safety courses
actions.description: Free, facilitated online courses in AI safety and AI governance, open to people without a technical background; a common first step toward working on catastrophic AI risk.
